cross.title: A GLIMPSE of Dark Matter: JWST Constraints on Early Structure Formation
cross.summary: While we have a solid understanding of how dark matter (DM) behaves during recombination ($z\sim 10^3$) and in the late universe ($z\lesssim$ a few), much less is known about intermediate times, when the first galaxies formed. These galaxies provide a powerful handle on DM through structure formation, as halos have to exist to host luminous sources. Here we use recent determinations of the UV luminosity function from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) GLIMPSE lensing program, along with legacy Hubble and Subaru data, to test the small-scale behavior of DM during the epoch of reionization ($z\sim 7$). Marginalizing over astrophysical uncertainties, we find the matter power spectrum to be consistent with the cold-DM prediction down to sub-Mpc scales, with 1$\sigma$ uncertainties of 0.2 dex at $k=3-9 \, \rm Mpc^{-1}$ and 0.5 dex at $k=9-27 \, \rm Mpc^{-1}$, the smallest scales probed at these early times. For thermal-relic warm DM we constrain $m_{\rm WDM} > 3.2\, \rm keV$ (95% CL), independent of lower-$z$ probes. Our results test small-scale structure formation in a new redshift window and demonstrate the promise of JWST to constrain the nature of DM.

cross.title: Seeing Unseen Gravitational Wave Inspirals at the Galactic Center
cross.summary: The Galactic Center is expected to host a population of extremely large mass-ratio inspirals (X-MRIs) migrating toward the supermassive black hole. We propose an observational approach utilizing the secular gravitational torque exerted by X-MRIs on the highly eccentric S-star S301. This approach is intrinsically limited by the stochastic nature of the surrounding stellar-mass black hole cusp. As S301 propagates through this granular medium, it experiences discrete gravitational encounters. Standard orbital fitting procedures inherently assume a smooth background potential; applying them to stochastic trajectories averages these discrete velocity discontinuities into a continuous secular drift. This introduces a systematic bias that mimics the X-MRI precession signal, invalidating traditional mass estimation techniques. To resolve this degeneracy, we implement a methodology based on the Wavelet Transform Modulus Maxima method to characterize the local Hölder regularity of the orbital motion. This model isolates the singular discontinuities induced by stellar-mass black hole encounters from the continuous torque of the X-MRI distribution, allowing for detection even when instantaneous accelerations are below the instrumental noise threshold. We demonstrate analytically that S301 is highly sensitive to the interior X-MRI population while remaining dynamically decoupled from the secular influence of the exterior cusp. Combining precision astrometry and radial velocity projections, we establish that a minimal population of two X-MRIs is detectable within a five to nine-year timeframe, allowing us to constrain the presence of an unseen orbiter population prior to the launch of space-based gravitational wave detectors.

cross.title: Combining Multiple Incomplete Astronomical Surveys to Estimate Galaxy Flux Distributions
cross.summary: In astrophysics, the distributions of fluxes or intensities of populations of sources provide insight into the structure and evolution of the universe. We propose a science-driven hierarchical Bayesian framework to estimate the X-ray flux distribution of a population of galaxies. The distribution is parameterized via a broken power law model, formulated as a mixture of Pareto distributions, and is fit using data from a combination of non-representative X-ray and optical surveys. Because fainter sources are less likely to be detected, astronomical surveys suffer from incompleteness at the low-intensity end, and dedicated survey simulations are used to study the resulting missing-data pattern and determine the form of corrections. We introduce a methodology to combine data from two (or more) surveys with different incompleteness functions. This allows us to leverage deeper surveys (e.g., optical) to more fully characterize the X-ray log(N)-log(S) (where fewer sources are detected). We take advantage of a well-calibrated characterization of the missing-data pattern, particularly in X-ray surveys, to make incompleteness corrections for sources that are not detected in either survey. The proposed model is validated using a simulation study designed to mimic the Chandra Deep Field South (CDF-S), demonstrating accurate recovery of the flux distribution even under high proportions of systematic incompleteness. Finally, we apply our proposed method to data from the CDF-S.

cross.title: Validating an X-ray-based method for identifying Fermi blazars
cross.summary: Context. Blazars are the main population of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) detected in gamma rays by Fermi. However, around 34% of Fermi sources remain unidentified, partly due to their large positional uncertainties, motivating multiwavelength methods to identify possible counterparts. Aims. We evaluate a method proposed to identify BL Lacertae (BL Lac) candidates among unidentified Fermi sources based on their X-ray properties, using Swift-XRT observations. Methods. We examined published optical spectra for an initial sample of 148 X-ray-selected candidates. We found 71 sources with spectra spatially consistent with the proposed associations and reassessed their classifications using standard blazar criteria. We then compared these classifications with the method's initial predictions. Results. Of the 71 proposed counterparts, 80.28% are classified as BL Lac objects and 87.32% as possible gamma-ray-emitting AGNs, supporting the effectiveness of the X-ray-based selection. We also identify four Seyfert galaxies, suggesting that the method is sensitive to this class despite its rarity among gamma-ray emitters. Conclusions. Our results show that X-ray observations are effective for selecting BL Lac candidates among unidentified Fermi sources and support future spectroscopic follow-up campaigns. The high fraction of BL Lacs and AGNs suggests that blazars may account for a substantial part of the unidentified gamma-ray population. The Seyfert identifications also raise questions about the origin of high-energy emission in AGNs not typically associated with relativistic jets, highlighting the need for further multiwavelength observations.

cross.title: Simulating and Characterizing Non-Gaussian Small-Scale Polarized Emission
cross.summary: Galactic foregrounds present a major challenge for cosmic microwave background (CMB) cosmology as their amplitudes exceed the target primordial $B$-mode signal. While small-scale interstellar medium (ISM) emission is expected to be highly complex, current foreground simulations cannot reproduce the filamentary, non-Gaussian features of ISM structure in a stochastic way. To address this gap, we introduce a framework for generating stochastic small-scale foreground emission, using polarized synchrotron observations as an example use case. This method is capable of producing many independent realizations that additionally inherit morphological information from large angular scales. The underlying structural complexity incorporates anisotropic, multifractal, and advected non-Gaussian features that are tunable with a small number of parameters that carry physical interpretations. Because standard power spectra do not describe the complex phase coherence required for the structural complexity, we evaluate the synthetic fields using higher-order statistics, demonstrating that the Minkowski functionals and structure functions partially capture varying degrees of non-Gaussianity. This work lays the necessary foundation for new foreground simulation suites with stochastic realizations of possible non-Gaussian structure.

cross.title: Cosmic rays in galaxy halos I: the circumgalactic transport rate and a dynamically significant cosmic-ray reservoir
cross.summary: Fermi-LAT observations imply that most of the cosmic rays (CRs) produced in normal star-forming galaxies escape from the discs where they are accelerated into the circumgalactic medium (CGM), but the subsequent evolution of those escaping CRs is unclear. Here we construct a simple semi-analytic model for their transport and loss, which we constrain by confronting the model with a series of observations: limits on CR energy densities in the outer Milky Way from Fermi-LAT, the isotropic gamma-ray background (IGRB), stacked CGM X-ray emission from eROSITA, and the requirement that the accumulated pressure of CRs in galaxy CGMs not be so large as to render them unstable. We show that these constraints can be jointly satisfied in only two scenarios: one where CRs diffuse quickly through the CGM and freely escape beyond it into the IGM, and another where the CR diffusion time out of halos is of order the Hubble time. In the latter scenario CRs accelerated by star formation naturally explain both the IGRB and the heat input required to maintain the temperature of the CGM against X-ray cooling, and their relatively slow transport means that roughly half of the CR energy injected into the CGM of an $L_\star$ halo over its star-formation history remains there at $z \simeq 0$. This makes CR pressure dynamically significant, and also means that a non-negligible part of the IGRB is produced by CRs in the Milky Way's own halo. We argue that this latter scenario is the more likely one, as it avoids the need to posit a second source for the IGRB that is coincidentally very close in both power and spectral shape to the contribution from star-forming discs.

cross.title: Numerical Simulations of the interaction between winds from tidal disruption event and supermassive black hole circumnuclear medium
cross.summary: The interaction between winds from tidal disruption event (TDE) and the circumnuclear medium (CNM) around supermassive black holes is believed to contribute to the radio emission of non-jetted TDEs. This model has been studied both analytically and numerically. In previous works, the properties of wind are usually set to be angle-independent. It is not clear to what extent the results deviate from those in the case where TDE wind properties are angle-dependent. We perform numerical simulations to investigate the effects of the angular distribution of wind properties on the radio light curve in the wind-CNM interaction model. We find that given that the wind mass and kinetic energy fixed, the radio light curve in the optically thin waveband significantly depends on the angle-dependence of wind properties. Even when the swept-up CNM mass is still less than the wind mass, a slight deceleration can affect the light curve. Changing the angular dependence of the wind properties causes the deceleration to vary across angles. Consequently, the final light curve--the time evolution of radiation integrated over all angles--would differ significantly from that predicted in models with a spatially uniform wind injection. This can result in a slower rise or a faster decline (depending on the CNM profile) than the analytical prediction, and can even turn the rise phase into a long-lasting plateau. Therefore, it is essential to carefully take into account the angular dependence of wind properties to study the wind-CNM interaction.

cross.title: PyMsOfa 2.0: A Pure-Python Implementation of the IAU Standards of Fundamental Astronomy Service
cross.summary: Astrometric calculations require authoritative algorithms so that every result is correct and reproducible. The Standards of Fundamental Astronomy (SOFA) service of the International Astronomical Union (IAU) provides such algorithms, officially released only in Fortran 77 and ANSI C. In an earlier paper we presented the first version of PyMsOfa, a Python package wrapping the SOFA C library. Here we present PyMsOfa 2.0, which re-implements the complete SOFA library in pure Python with NumPy. All 247 official SOFA routines are ported directly to Python, requiring no compilation of any external C library and running identically on Linux, Windows, and macOS. The routines operate on NumPy arrays, so arguments can be processed in batch, which is convenient for survey pipelines and Monte Carlo simulations. The package also provides an extension module with validated models not yet part of the official SOFA release, such as the improved precession--nutation model IAU 2006$_{J_2}$/2000A$_{R26}$. The reimplementation reproduces the official SOFA algorithms: all constants, series, and coefficients are taken unchanged from the SOFA source files, and routine names differ only by the pym prefix. We verify every routine against the official SOFA C release: most reproduce the C results to machine precision, the remainder within the accuracy tolerance stated in the SOFA documentation. The package has been applied to Gaia astrometric reduction and used in astrometric studies of the Closeby Habitable Exoplanet Survey (CHES) mission, and is available through PyPI, GitHub, and Zenodo.

cross.title: Migration Traps as Variability Attractors. II. Nonmonotonic X-Ray Timing Signatures of Embedded Stellar-Mass Black Holes in AGN Disks
cross.summary: Stellar-mass black holes (sBHs) embedded in active galactic nucleus (AGN) disks may affect X-ray variability through magnetic reconnection. As sBHs migrate and accumulate near migration traps, they disturb the disk magnetic field and trigger reconnection events that heat the disk and eject plasma into the overlying corona. The injected plasma dissipates kinetic energy and can trigger the release of magnetic energy already stored in the corona. We calculate the resulting coronal X-ray emission and the disk ultraviolet (UV) variability, including the disk thermal response and reprocessing of incident X-rays. We find that embedded sBHs can initially enhance short-timescale X-ray variability, but the variability becomes suppressed as more sBHs accumulate in the disk. At higher mass accretion rates through AGN disks, this suppression appears earlier. As sBH-associated reconnection events become more frequent, their active regions increasingly overlap, reducing the magnetic energy available to each event from the corona. We also find that variations in the disk ultraviolet (UV) emission follow the X-ray variations with a shorter delay than in the model without sBHs. These results suggest that a growing population of embedded sBHs does not necessarily produce stronger short-timescale X-ray variability.

cross.title: Nongravitational Motion of 3I/ATLAS Far from the Sun: Robust Detection, Weak Constraints on the Activity Law
cross.summary: 3I/ATLAS provides an unprecedented astrometric data set for studying nongravitational (NG) effects in an interstellar object, but existing orbital solutions depend strongly on assumptions regarding the heliocentric activity law and the treatment of the astrometric data. We investigate the extent to which astrometric observations constrain the heliocentric dependence of the NG activity function, focusing on the identifiability of different functional forms of $g(r)$ within standard NG orbit-determination frameworks. Astrometric observations obtained at heliocentric distances larger than 3.49 au before perihelion and 2.67 au after perihelion were analysed. Purely gravitational and nongravitational orbital solutions were determined using several activity laws, including the standard water-ice sublimation law and flatter more volatile ice prescriptions. The resulting residual distributions were evaluated using normality tests and analyses of temporal trends in the observed-minus-calculated residuals. The distant pre-perihelion observations are well described by a purely gravitational (GR) orbit, whereas the distant post-perihelion data exhibit a statistically significant non-Gaussian residual distribution under the GR model. When the distant pre- and post-perihelion observations are combined, nongravitational acceleration becomes clearly detectable through a significant reduction in the residual rms and the disappearance of systematic residual trends. However, the astrometric data do not uniquely distinguish between the tested activity laws: standard water-ice, more volatile and extreme volatile prescriptions produce statistically comparable orbital fits despite their markedly different heliocentric dependences. The existence of nongravitational acceleration is therefore considerably better constrained by astrometry than its physical origin or heliocentric dependence.

cross.title: Understanding the origin of silver in metal-poor stars based on the non-local thermodynamic equilibrium analysis of Ag I lines
cross.summary: Silver is a poorly observed neutron-capture element, and understanding its Galactic production history requires accurate abundances for stellar samples covering a broad metallicity range. We refined the method for calculating stellar Ag abundances by considering the non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) line formation for Ag I. A comprehensive model atom of silver was built from the atomic data available in the literature, including recent data on inelastic Ag I + H I collisions. We derived abundances using the high-resolution spectra and the synthetic spectrum method with the one-dimensional model atmospheres. From two Ag I lines in the solar spectrum we obtained the NLTE abundances log epsilon = 1.15 and 1.10 for different treatments of collisions with hydrogen atoms. The NLTE abundances of Ag were determined for the first time for 41 stars in the -2.74 <= [Fe/H] <= -0.56 metallicity range. The NLTE abundance corrections for Ag I 3382 A were found to be larger for the giants (up to 0.92~dex) than the dwarfs (up to 0.51~dex). In NLTE, Ag in our sample stars is enhanced relatively to Fe and the [Ag/Fe] Galactic trend is very similar to that for [Eu/Fe]; the [Ag/Eu], [Ag/Ba], and [Ag/Sr] abundance ratios of the r-II stars CS22892-052 and CS31082-001 agree very well with the r-process model of Prantzos et al. (2020); the -1.6 < [Fe/H] <= -0.56 stars have close-to-solar [Ag/Eu] ratios. We conclude that production of silver was dominated by the main r-process throughout the metallicity range we investigated, with the main s-process contribution of not larger than 20% for [Fe/H] > -1.6.

cross.title: Atmospheric Parameter Determination of RR Lyrae Stars With Mephisto Multi-band Photometry
cross.summary: Phase-resolved atmospheric parameters of pulsating stars, including RR Lyrae stars and Cepheids, are essential for studying stellar structure and pulsation physics and for establishing accurate stellar benchmarks for Galactic structure and assembly history. We present a photometric framework that simultaneously infers Teff, log g, and [Fe/H] from Mephisto multi-epoch, multi-band (u, v, g, r, i, z) photometry. A supervised neural-network forward model is built by training on synthetic colors derived from theoretical stellar atmosphere models. It reproduces the synthetic colors to a precision of 0.01 per cent. The model is applied to observed multi-epoch colors to derive phase-dependent atmospheric parameters. We apply the method to six RRab and four RRc stars in three globular clusters observed with Mephisto. We find typical per-phase uncertainties of about 62 K in effective temperature (Teff), 0.10 dex in surface gravity (log g), and 0.16 dex in metallicity ([Fe/H]). Repeated measurements across the pulsation cycle reduce the typical formal uncertainty of the final [Fe/H] estimates to roughly 0.03 dex. A sensitivity analysis indicates that the five Mephisto colors provide distinct and complementary constraints on the three stellar atmospheric parameters: (u-v) provides robust constraints on log g, (v-g) is informative for estimating [Fe/H], and (u-v), (v-g), (g-r), (r-i), and (i-z) all provide information on Teff. The results demonstrate that Mephisto multi-epoch, multi-band photometry can deliver precise, cost-effective phase-resolved atmospheric parameters for RR Lyrae stars, offering an efficient way to construct large samples of stellar benchmarks for studies of stellar pulsation physics and Galactic structure and evolution.

cross.title: Black Hole Spin Evolution in Magnetized Accretion Flows
cross.summary: Black hole (BH) spin grows as accretion supplies angular momentum and decreases as magnetically driven jets remove it, driving the BH toward an equilibrium spin, $a_{\rm \star; eq}$. Existing estimates of $a_{\rm \star; eq}$ rely on general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations with fixed BH mass and spin, and cover only the extreme limits of horizon magnetic flux $\phi\rightarrow0$ and magnetically arrested disks (MADs), $\phi\approx\phi_{\rm MAD}$. We evolve the BH mass and spin in long 3D GRMHD simulations of radiatively inefficient accretion flows aligned or anti-aligned with the BH spin. We find the spin-up parameter as a function of BH spin and $\phi/\phi_{\rm MAD}$, and derive the equilibrium spin as a continuous function of flux, $a_{\rm \star; eq}(\phi/\phi_{\rm MAD})$. The equilibrium spin falls steeply with flux, from $a_{\rm \star; eq}\approx0.9$ in weakly magnetized flows through $a_{\rm \star; eq}(\phi/\phi_{\rm MAD}=0.5)\approx0.5$ to $a_{\rm \star; eq}(\phi/\phi_{\rm MAD}=1)\approx0.06$ in sustained MADs. In weakly magnetized flows, a slowly spinning BH must accrete at least its initial mass to reach equilibrium, whereas MADs spin down rapidly rotating BHs after accreting less than half of it. However, as the BH grows, the growing gravitational radius and enhanced inflow reduce $\phi/\phi_{\rm MAD}$, driving disks whose magnetic-flux supply cannot keep pace out of the MAD state and allowing the BH to transition from spin-down to spin-up. The final spin thus depends on both the magnetic flux history and the accreted mass. We discuss implications for a variety of BH-powered engines and provide a subgrid prescription for galaxy-scale simulations and population studies.

cross.title: Infrared spectroscopy of the longest-period Galactic Mira variables from Palomar Gattini-IR: Identification of a candidate thermally pulsing Super-Asymptotic Giant Branch star
cross.summary: The population of extremely long-period Mira variables in the Milky Way remains poorly characterized. Their rarity and heavy circumstellar obscuration have precluded systematic studies in optical surveys, yet they are expected to trace the most massive stars evolving through the Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB). We present IRTF/SpeX spectroscopy of the longest-period ($P\gtrsim1000$ d) Galactic Mira variables identified with the Palomar Gattini-IR survey. Twelve of thirteen targets exhibit characteristics consistent with massive O-rich AGB stars. In contrast, one peculiar source IRAS 19552+3142 exhibits i) a large-amplitude ($\Delta J\gtrsim2$ mag) pulsations with $P\approx1060$ d, ii) strong C$_2$ and CO molecular bands indicating C/O$\gtrsim1$, and iii) SiC emission at $\approx11.3\,\mu$m in archival mid-infrared spectra. Its spectroscopically confirmed chemistry makes it the longest period C-rich Galactic Mira variable known; together with the rarity of similar objects, this source is difficult to reconcile with standard massive AGB evolution where hot-bottom burning maintains an O-rich surface composition. Instead, its properties may be explained by super-AGB evolution where dredge-out episodes produce a C-rich surface and circumstellar material. Its high luminosity ($M_{[4.5]}\lesssim-10$ mag), red color ($[3.6] - [4.5]\gtrsim2.0$ mag), and high mass-loss rate ($\gtrsim 10^{-4} \mathrm{M_\odot yr^{-1}}$) resemble extreme AGB star progenitors of intermediate-luminosity red transients in nearby galaxies and a known chemically peculiar super-AGB star candidate in the Small Magellanic Cloud. IRAS 19552+3142 may thus provide a rare look at a Galactic super-AGB star in the thermally pulsing phase. Our results motivate improved theoretical predictions and long-baseline infrared searches for these short-lived, dust-enshrouded endpoints of stellar evolution.

cross.title: UnEZ: A Fully Unsupervised Self-Templating Neural Network for Redshift and Line Strength Estimation
cross.summary: As spectroscopic surveys grow, estimating galaxy properties such as metallicity, star formation rate, and redshift becomes computationally cumbersome. Methods of estimating such properties rely on template spectra or curated redshift catalogs, which fail to represent the diversity of objects seen in large-scale surveys. We present UnEZ, a fully unsupervised, physics-informed machine learning model that can predict spectroscopic redshifts and line strengths with no prior redshift or line strength labels. An encoder predicts emission and absorption line amplitudes/widths, and a fixed deterministic decoder constructs a unique template, estimated redshift, redshift confidence curve, and spectral model. UnEZ was tested on the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Data Release 18 due to its large dataset and thoroughly vetted redshift catalog which serves as an independent benchmark. Despite the lack of templates, line strength labels, or redshift labels, UnEZ's performance competes with modern redshift estimation algorithms. At SNR > 10, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 0.459% and a normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD) of $1.237 \times 10^{-4}$. At SNR > 3, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 3.89% and an NMAD of $1.471 \times 10^{-4}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate how UnEZ's line strength and redshift predictions can be utilized for various purposes such as constructing template spectra required in traditional redshift estimation algorithms. UnEZ illustrates how a fully unsupervised neural network can allow redshift, among other galaxy properties, to emerge naturally from the spectra themselves, providing a template-free, label-free approach that scales to the demands of future surveys.

cross.title: The Bochum Survey of the Southern Galactic Disk: IV. Multi-Band Photometry
cross.summary: The Southern Galactic Disk Survey (GDS) monitored a mosaic of 268 fields along a $6^\circ$-wide stripe in the southern galactic disk from September 2010 to September 2019. These fields were observed between 21 and 407 times simultaneously in $r'$ ($8\,\mathrm{mag} \lesssim r' \lesssim 18\,\mathrm{mag}$) and $i'$ ($7\,\mathrm{mag} \lesssim i' \lesssim 17\,\mathrm{mag}$), supplemented by between 2 and 147 observations in each of the bands $U$, $B$, $V$, and $z'$. Here we present the matched multi-band catalogue, which integrates photometry and light curve data from all bands, containing photometry for almost 21.7 million Gaia DR3 sources, of which $113\,449$ are identified as variables. We give an overview of the survey's variable content with respect to its main characteristics and known variability type classifications. The comparison with the cross-match catalogue of Gaia DR3 sources with variables from the literature compiled by Gavras et al. (2023) and the International Variable Star Index (VSX) indicates that approximately $40\,\%$ of the variable sources remain unclassified in terms of variability type. Light curves for all of these sources are contained in the GDS data catalogues, available via the German Astrophysical Virtual Observatory (GAVO), and can contribute to their classification.

cross.title: A morpho-kinematic view of the Necklace nebula
cross.summary: We present a morpho-kinematic study of the Necklace Nebula based on spatially resolved spectroscopic observations and 3D modeling performed with the SHAPE software. The nebula is characterized by an equatorial disrupted ring accompanied by bipolar outflows. The geometry and velocity field of these different components are derived from the comparison between observed and synthetic images and position-velocity diagrams. The best model successfully reproduces the main morphological and kinematic features of the nebula, allowing us to constrain its 3D structure. We confirm that the disrupted ring is tilted about 60° from the plane of the sky, but the bipolar outflows are inclined by 46° with respect to the line of sight. This situation might indicate that the bipolar structures are not simple extensions of the equatorial ring, but instead correspond to a distinct mass-ejection event. The slight misalignment between these two components suggests either precession of the ejection axis, a temporal change in the dominant mass-loss geometry, or a misalignment in the magnetic field. Given that the Necklace Nebula hosts a close binary central star and is a well-established post-common envelope planetary nebula, our results support a scenario in which binary interaction plays a central role in shaping its morphology, even before the common envelope phase.

cross.title: The Korean Space Telescope (KST): A Dedicated Space Observatory for the Dark Universe
cross.summary: The Korean Space Telescope (KST) is a next-generation 1.4-meter wide-field space observatory, a dedicated probe of the dark sector. Its single instrument provides diffraction-limited visible imaging (~0.15 arcsec in the optical) together with simultaneous near-infrared (R ~ 100) slitless spectrophotometry, so that every detected source is observed in the NIR by the survey itself, with spectral information delivered at a resolution set by its brightness (full R ~ 100 typing at the bright end, synthetic medium-band or broadband photometry below it) and with no separate follow-up, a capability decisive for time-domain science. With it, KST addresses the three outstanding questions of dark physics in concert: the dynamics of dark energy, the nature of dark matter, and gravitational-wave dark sirens as independent cosmological rulers. KST combines measurements of expansion and structure growth to test dark-energy models. A two-tiered "Wedding Cake" strategy (2,000 deg^2 Wide plus 10 deg^2 cluster-targeted Deep Survey) combines weak lensing, baryon acoustic oscillations, and a near-infrared-standardized Type Ia supernova Hubble diagram to constrain dark energy at its pivot redshift (sigma(w_p) ~ 0.03); maps dark matter from cluster cores to galactic substructure to test cold dark matter against warm and self-interacting alternatives; and builds a deep near-infrared host catalog for a distance-ladder-independent H_0 from dark sirens. The same data yield a Legacy Science portfolio (galaxy evolution, active galactic nuclei, exoplanets, and the Milky Way) at no additional observing cost. As Korea's first dedicated astrophysics space mission, KST occupies a niche complementary to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Euclid, and Roman.

cross.title: A Low-Dimensional Chemical Representation of High-Resolution Stellar Disk Spectra: Residual Abundance Signatures
cross.summary: Stellar abundances are generated by complex chemical enrichment pathways yet show strong correlation structure. We test how well high-quality spectra of low-alpha disk stars can be reconstructed using low-dimensional models. By validating model performance in flux space, we quantify and locate where residual information persists. Using HARPS spectra (R = 115,000, SNR > 100) and labels derived with Korg, we train generative models (The Cannon) conditioned on stellar parameters Teff, log(g), [M/H], vsini, and vmic, and three abundance labels, [Ti/H], [Y/H], and [Nd/H], representing distinct nucleosynthetic families. Evaluating model performance on unseen test stars through flux residuals, the model reproduces the global spectra to a median residual amplitude of 0.3%. Deviations in 15 absorption features for unlabelled elements are typically < 0.7%. Residuals of ~1% correspond to abundance differences of 0.01-0.05 dex. Degrading the spectra to medium resolution (R = 28,000) decreases the median residual amplitude from 0.3% to 0.2%, redistributing the residual signal over the instrumental line profile. Our publicly available model reproduces features from 29 elements to sub-percent precision across -1.13 < [M/H] < 0.29. This demonstrates that the dominant chemical variation encoded in low-alpha disk spectra can be captured by a low-dimensional model, while weaker chemical information remains encoded in flux residuals. High-resolution, high-SNR spectra (R ~ 100,000, SNR > 100) are essential to resolve the hierarchical layers of chemical information beyond this low-dimensional structure. The model provides a benchmark for assessing the chemical information accessible to current surveys like 4MOST and GALAH 2, as well as upcoming facilities like VLT/HRMOS and GMT/G-CLEF.

cross.title: Mapping cluster angular momentum with the rotational kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect
cross.summary: Galaxy clusters carry angular momentum. If the intracluster gas rotates coherently, the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) effect imprints a dipole on the microwave sky centered on the cluster. We show that microwave maps alone can be used to reconstruct a noisy vector field tracing the projected angular momentum of the ionized gas. We present an optimal multifrequency matched filter (MMF) that isolates the rotational kSZ (rkSZ) signal from the much larger miscentered thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect, cosmic microwave, and infrared background contributions, improving on both real-space oriented stacking and matched filtering of maps cleaned with full-sky multifrequency weights. For the rkSZ profile, we introduce a simple model for coherent intracluster gas rotation and validate it against TNG-Cluster and TNG300-1. The model consists of differentially rotating concentric shells with constant equatorial tangential velocity, characterized by a mass- and redshift-indepedent tangential-to-circular velocity ratio of $v_{\rm tan}/V_{c,200c}=0.18$. Using this model, we forecast single-cluster signal-to-noise (SNR) as a function of mass and redshift for Simons Observatory; cross-correlation with an external catalog of rotation proxies yields a cumulative detection SNR. For an idealized mass-limited catalog with perfectly known spin directions, the cumulative SNR of our optimal MMF reaches $\approx 53$, $25$, and $6$ when including all clusters above $\log_{10}(M_{200c}/M_\odot)>14$, 14.5, and 15, respectively. This work provides a practical framework for CMB measurements of intracluster gas rotation, with applications to the rotational contribution to non-thermal pressure in cluster mass calibration, as well as spin alignments and clustering biases.

cross.title: Four-hundred Very Metal-poor Stars Studied with LAMOST and Subaru. IV. Heavy Element Enhanced Stars
cross.summary: We perform a homogeneous analysis of 82 heavy-element-enhanced metal-poor stars from the\\ LAMOST/Subaru sample, including 64 $r$-process-enhanced stars, 2 limited-$r$ stars, and 16 stars exhibiting significant or moderate carbon enhancement (comprising 9 $s$-process-enhanced, 2 $r$-process-enhanced, 2 $r$/$s$, and 3 $r$+$s$ stars). Systematic differences in $\mathrm{[X/Eu]}$ between $r$-I and $r$-II stars, together with their distinct dynamical properties, suggest that $r$-II stars likely formed in low-mass dwarf galaxies where contamination from additional nucleosynthetic channels was minimal. We have also discovered a number of peculiar objects. We identify an extremely metal-poor $r$-II star, J1158+0734 ($\mathrm{[Fe/H]}$ = -2.93), whose enhanced Zn abundance ($\mathrm{[Zn/Fe]}$ = +0.67) is best explained by yields from a high-energy, massive core-collapse supernova. The surface abundances of $s$-process-enhanced stars exhibit pronounced dispersion, consistent with enrichment from AGB progenitors with diverse properties. Notably, one star, J2256+0215, reveals compelling evidence for additional evolutionary mixing, as indicated by its unusually low carbon abundance ($\mathrm{[C/Fe]}$ = +0.08) and extremely low $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratio of 2.33. Additionally, we identify 3 $r$+$s$ stars whose abundance patterns reveal combined contributions from both the $r$- and $s$-processes. We further propose a modified diagnostic scheme for the identification of CEMP-$r$+$s$ stars, defined as: -0.2 $\leqslant$ $\mathrm{[La/Nd]}$ $\leqslant$ 0.2 and -0.5 $\leqslant$ $\mathrm{[Eu/Nd]}$ $\leqslant$ 0.0.

cross.title: Extracting non-Gaussian information of line-intensity maps with weighted skew spectra
cross.summary: The bispectrum of line-intensity maps carries cosmological and astrophysical information beyond the power spectrum, but its large data vector hampers the analysis of survey data. Skew spectra address this by compressing the bispectrum into a handful of power-spectrum-like observables, cross-spectra of the observed field with filtered squares of it. We present the first application of optimally weighted skew spectra to line-intensity mapping of galaxy-hosted emission, where all clustering and shot-noise terms are luminosity weighted and the mean intensity is unknown. We perform idealized real-space Fisher forecasts for a SPHEREx-like survey of H$\alpha$ emission at $0.2 \lesssim z \lesssim 4.6$, in its deep fields and in a noisier all-sky configuration. First, the compression carries over to intensity maps: on perturbative scales and for a fixed redshift evolution of the emitters, four skew spectra, one of them matched to the shot noise, recover the bispectrum constraints on biases, shot noise and cosmological parameters to within a few percent. Second, the joint analysis of the power spectrum and the skew spectra measures the ratios of the second-order biases to the linear bias in each redshift bin. Within a bin the biases are degenerate with the unknown mean intensity, but their ratios are not, so their redshift evolution is measured without a model for the emitters. For emission that depends on halo mass alone, these ratios are determined by luminosity-weighted averages of the halo biases, so their evolution can test the halo-emission connection, including dependence on assembly history or environment. The bias ratios are not accessible to the tree-level real-space power spectrum alone. At $z \lesssim 3$ an all-sky SPHEREx-like configuration can detect departures of order $0.1$ in the bias ratios at $3\sigma$, while deeper fields perform better in the highest-redshift bins.

cross.title: Toward a Complete Interpretation of Global 21 cm Absorption Signals Using the Radio CMB
cross.summary: The global 21 cm signal is among the most direct probes of cosmic dawn, encoding information about when the first stars formed and how efficiently they heated their surroundings. However, such measurements are limited by bright Galactic foregrounds, ionospheric effects, and instrumental systematics. Even a confident detection would face a further obstacle: the brightness temperature depends on the spin temperature of the gas and the temperature of the radio background only through a single combination, so anomalous signals such as the EDGES (Bowman et al. 2018) absorption trough admit both cold gas and excess radio background interpretations. Recently, Holder et al. 2026 showed that resonant 21 cm absorption by high-redshift neutral hydrogen imprints an excess optical depth on CMB anisotropies at radio wavelengths, which depends on the spin temperature alone. Here we propose combining a measurement of the CMB hydrogen optical depth with the global signal to break this degeneracy, isolating the radio background temperature without the need for astrophysical modelling. Forecasting four interferometric configurations, we find that a compact $55 \times 55$ array of 6 m dishes observing for 4000 hours can establish an EDGES-like optical depth at $4.2\sigma$, while fiducial cosmic dawn histories require roughly an order of magnitude more collecting area. This constitutes a model-independent route to interpreting any global 21 cm detection.

cross.title: UNIONS: Red and blue alignments of DESI DR1 galaxies
cross.summary: Intrinsic alignments (IA) of galaxies are a dominant source of systematics in weak-lensing cosmological analyses, and direct measurements on spectroscopic samples are the primary source of priors on their amplitude. We measure the IA of galaxies from the first data release (DR1) of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) as a function of colour, stellar mass, and halo mass, by cross-correlating the DESI spectroscopic catalogues with the weak-lensing shape catalogue of the Ultraviolet Near-Infrared Optical Northern Survey (UNIONS) over up to 2400 deg$^2$. We fit the three-dimensional galaxy-galaxy and galaxy-shape multipoles of the DESI BGS, LRG, and ELG samples, split by colour and stellar mass, with the non-linear linear alignment (NLA) and the tidal alignment and tidal torquing (TATT) models. Halo masses are measured for the BGS red sample from galaxy-galaxy lensing and extended to the LRGs through the resulting stellar-to-halo mass relation. Red galaxies are strongly and radially aligned, but their alignment amplitude is not a single power law of halo mass between $6\times10^{11}$ and $3\times10^{13}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$: it is nearly flat at low mass and rises steeply above a break at $1.3\times10^{13}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$. Massive blue BGS galaxies instead show a tangential alignment, detected at $3.3\sigma$, to our knowledge the most significant detection of a non-zero alignment of blue galaxies to date, while the low-mass blue BGS galaxies and the ELGs are consistent with zero. At our current precision, the data do not favour TATT over NLA.

cross.title: An Empirically Calibrated [C II] Luminosity-Halo Mass Relation for Line Intensity Mapping
cross.summary: Millimeter-wave line intensity mapping aims to observe the high-redshift universe through the 158 $\mu$m fine-structure line of [C II], the brightest far-infrared line of star-forming galaxies. Whether a [C II] experiment at $z>4$ measures the clustering of large-scale structure, which carries rich cosmological information, rather than the shot noise of the emitters depends on the amplitude and the shape of the [C II] power spectrum. Forecasts often build the power spectrum from a halo mass--luminosity relation, $L(M_h)$, chained from scaling relations measured in other regimes or read off simulations, without a quantified uncertainty. We instead calibrate a double power-law $L(M_h,z)$ on [C II] data alone: the mean [C II] intensity from tomographic cross-correlation at $0.4<z<4.2$ and the luminosity-function measurements and limits at $z\simeq0$ and $4.3\lesssim z\lesssim8$. The four parameters of the double power law are fitted at $z=4.5$ and $5.5$ separately, with no assumption about their evolution, and then jointly across $0<z<7$, and we examine how the uncertainty depends on the modeling assumptions. The shape of the power spectrum is settled by the existing data. The clustering peak stands a factor of $45\,(23$-$93)$ and $64\,(38$-$112)$ above the shot-noise floor at $z=4.5$ and $5.5$, and the two cross at $k_c\simeq0.37$ and $0.44\,h$Mpc$^{-1}$. The amplitude is known less well, the clustering power to $0.5-0.6$ dex and the shot noise to $0.7-0.9$ dex. The results show that the signal comes from halos accessible by current galaxy surveys, those that host the Lyman-break galaxies and Ly$\alpha$ emitters at these redshifts. The luminosity-weighted bias is relatively high, with values of $4-5$.

cross.title: The unresolved high-mass frontier of the black hole Fundamental Plane
cross.summary: Accreting black holes follow a Fundamental Plane (FP) linking radio and X-ray luminosities to black hole mass, but whether this relation changes in the ultramassive regime, above $\sim10^{10}\,\Msun$, remains unresolved. Brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) provide the most direct access to this regime, although earlier claims of enhanced radio emission relied largely on heterogeneous nuclear measurements and black hole masses inferred from host-galaxy proxies. We recalibrate the forward FP using galaxies with direct dynamical mass measurements and reassess the evidence for a high-mass radio excess using the available BCG data. We find that the archival proxy-mass sample cannot uniquely establish such an excess because the inferred signal remains sensitive to the mass calibration and radio-selection properties of the sample. Using mock observing programs, we further show that the predictive width measured from existing observations makes a high-mass transition difficult to both detect and localize with present samples. The existing data therefore provide no compelling evidence for a distinct high-mass branch of the FP. Resolving this question will require a substantially larger, uniformly selected sample of galaxies with direct black hole masses and matched, preferably quasi-simultaneous, nuclear radio and X-ray measurements. A focused pilot survey of several dozen direct-mass systems would provide a practical first step toward establishing whether the required precision is achievable.

cross.title: The Conditional CMB Visibility of High-Redshift X-Ray Cavities in Galaxy clusters
cross.summary: At high redshift, the cosmic microwave background (CMB) both cools relativistic leptons and provides seed photons for inverse-Compton (IC) X-ray emission. These two effects link the particle content of a bubble directly to the soft X-ray depression used to identify a cavity. We derive a physical criterion connecting lepton cooling, bubble volume, enthalpy evolution, and 0.5--2 keV X-ray visibility, while separating intrinsic filling of the X-ray depression from detector-dependent cavity recovery. For uncooled electron populations described by a power law with spectral index $s=2.5$, minimum Lorentz factor $100\leq\gamma_{\min}\leq1000$, and maximum Lorentz factor $\gamma_{\max}=10^5$, the measured atmosphere of the testbed high-redshift cluster SPT-CL J2215$-$3537 requires 0.6--1.2\% of the pressure in radiating leptons to fill the soft-band deficit. Across the full tested ranges of $s$, $\gamma_{\min}$, and atmospheric properties, the required fraction is 0.2--3.7\%. Complete loss of this component reduces the enthalpy by less than 3\% relative to an otherwise identical adiabatic bubble at the same pressure. A low-cutoff control with $\gamma_{\min}=10$ and $s=3$ instead requires 18.9\%, identifying the poorly constrained low-energy spectrum as the main physical uncertainty. For a fixed atmosphere and spectrum, the required fraction scales as $(1+z)^{-4}$. The declining-pressure tracks show that the X-ray deficit can cross the adopted detection threshold while the enthalpy deficit remains below 0.4\%; the time of this transition depends on the assumed pressure history. Thus, high-redshift cavity visibility depends on both the surrounding atmosphere and the pressure-carrying particle spectrum. This criterion provides the physical basis for an instrument-specific recovery analysis.

cross.title: The $δ$ Scuti instability strip and period-luminosity relation as seen by TESS and Gaia DR3
cross.summary: We present an asteroseismic survey of 1,526,218 A- and F-type stars in and around the $\delta$ Scuti instability strip using TESS 10-minute cadence data, which resolve the full $\delta$ Scuti pulsation spectra across nearly the entire sky. We derive homogeneous stellar parameters from Gaia DR3 parallaxes and archival photometry, with temperatures that agree with interferometry to within ~300 K. A Positive--Unlabelled classifier identifies 156,706 $\delta$ Scuti pulsators, which on average rotate significantly faster than non-variable A-type stars. Within the instability strip in the $T_{eff}$--$\log L$ plane, the pulsator fraction peaks at 30% over the full sample and rises to 80% in the brightest magnitude bins. Detection sensitivity therefore accounts for much, but not all, of the apparent impurity of the strip. Our period--luminosity relation agrees with previous determinations, and we recast it as a scale-invariant period--density relation that connects directly to the pulsation constant. We find that the secondary ridge in these relations is probably a combination of several overtone modes. The $\delta$ Scuti stars closest to the fundamental ridge have systematically lower rotational velocities and occupy a distinct region of the instability strip. Finally, a cross-match with a Gaia catalog of open clusters reveals a correlation between the mean pulsation frequency of $\delta$ Scuti stars and cluster age, suggesting a new ensemble asteroseismic age indicator for young stellar populations.

repl.title: Modeling the Ages and Chemical Abundances of Elliptical Galaxies
repl.summary: Spectroscopic studies of elliptical galaxies show that their stellar population ages, mean metallicity, and $\alpha$-enhancement traced by [Mg/Fe] all increase with galaxy stellar mass or velocity dispersion. We use one-zone galactic chemical evolution (GCE) models with a flexible star formation history (SFH) to model the age, [Mg/H], and [Mg/Fe] inferred from simple stellar population (SSP) fits to observed ellipticals at $z \sim 0$ and $z \sim 0.7$. We show that an SSP fit to the spectrum computed from a full GCE model gives ages and abundances close to the light-weighted, logarithmically averaged values of the composite stellar population, <age>, <[Mg/H]>, and <[Mg/Fe]>. With supernova Mg and Fe yields fixed to values motivated by Milky Way stellar populations, we find that predicted <[Mg/H]>-<age> and <[Mg/Fe]>-<age> relations are surprisingly insensitive to SFH parameters: older galaxies have higher <[Mg/Fe]>, but the detailed form of the SFH has limited impact. The star formation efficiency and outflow efficiency affect the early and late evolution of <[Mg/H]>, respectively; explaining observed trends requires higher star formation efficiency and lower outflows in more massive galaxies. With core collapse supernova yields calibrated to the plateau [Mg/Fe]$_{\rm cc} \approx0.45$ observed in many Milky Way studies, our models underpredict the observed <[Mg/Fe]> ratios of ellipticals by 0.05-0.1 dex. Increasing the core collapse yield ratio to [Mg/Fe]$_{\rm cc} = 0.55$ improves the agreement, though the models still lie below the data. We discuss potential resolutions of this discrepancy, including the possibility that many ellipticals terminate their star formation with a self-enriching, terminating burst that reduces the light-weighted age and boosts <[Mg/Fe]>.

repl.title: A prevalent population of normal-mass central black holes in high-redshift massive galaxies
repl.summary: Understanding the co-evolution of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and their host galaxies is crucial for explaining how feedback from accreting black holes regulates star formation and shapes the growth of galaxies across cosmic time. However, measurements of this co-evolution in the early Universe, as traced by the black hole mass - stellar mass relation ($M_{\rm BH} - M_\star$), are subject to strong selection biases: SMBHs that are overly luminous and massive relative to their hosts are preferentially detected, particularly in the more abundant low-mass galaxies. To mitigate these biases, we conduct a systematic search for broad-line active galactic nuclei (AGN) in 117 spectroscopically confirmed massive galaxies at $z\sim3-5$, using deep JWST imaging and spectroscopic surveys conducted to date. We identify 20 moderate-luminosity AGNs with a mean $M_{\rm BH}/M_\star$ of $\sim0.1\%$, consistent with the local value. By reconstructing their mass ratios back to $z\sim6$, we infer that a substantial population of SMBHs with normal mass ratios was already in place within the first billion years of cosmic history, but has been largely overlooked by existing surveys. Together with the overmassive black holes reported in previous studies, our findings suggest diverse pathways for SMBH formation and growth in the early Universe. In addition, we find comparable $M_{\rm BH}/M_\star$ ratios in star-forming and quiescent host galaxies, suggesting that the formation of massive quiescent galaxies does not necessarily require an overmassive black hole, contrary to common theoretical expectations.

repl.title: From ASTRID to BRAHMA -- The role of overmassive black holes in little red dots in cosmological simulations
repl.summary: We investigate the origin of Little Red Dots (LRDs) using a realization of the BRAHMA cosmological hydrodynamic simulation that produces overmassive black holes at $z \sim 4\text{-}8$. We generate mock JWST observations by modeling galaxy spectral energy distributions (including dust attenuation) together with AGN emission using cloudy-based templates, and test whether such systems reproduce the observed LRD population. We consider both a standard low-redshift AGN emission model and a gas-enshrouded AGN emission model, in which the AGN is embedded within unresolved dense gas that produces a strong Balmer break, and find that LRDs emerge in significantly larger numbers with the latter model. Assuming that all AGN reside in this gas-enshrouded phase, we recover LRD number densities ($\Phi \sim 2 \times 10^{-4}~\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$), close to the observed abundance. This implies an effective gas-enshrouded duty cycle approaching unity, which is not predicted by current theoretical models. Current JWST constraints on the high-z black hole mass function suggest that this tension may arise from a deficit of low-mass ($M_{\rm BH}\lesssim10^7~M_\odot$) LRDs in BRAHMA. Applying the same gas-enshrouded model to the ASTRID simulation, which lacks overmassive black holes, we find that the LRD abundance remains $\gtrsim2~\rm dex$ below observations. Overall, while the overmassive black holes in this BRAHMA realization substantially enhance the production of LRD-like systems, reproducing the observed LRD abundance requires them to reside in dense gas environments with unrealistically high duty cycles. We therefore conclude that overmassive black holes are unlikely to be the sole origin of the observed JWST LRD population, and may instead account for only a subset of these systems.

repl.title: The Kinematically Hot, Extremely Metal-Poor C-19 Stellar Stream in DESI DR2
repl.summary: Stellar streams are the result of a host galaxy's gravitational potential tidally disrupting satellite dwarf galaxies and globular clusters (GCs), causing them to grow leading and trailing tidal tails. The C-19 stellar stream is an extremely metal-poor stellar population, showing chemical abundance patterns characteristic of a globular cluster. However, its large velocity dispersion is difficult to reconcile with a conventional, purely baryonic, disrupting-GC progenitor. Current techniques for stream characterization are primarily applied to Gaia DR3, relying heavily on proper motion measurements. Using the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), which provides radial velocities and metallicites for over 10 million stars reaching significantly fainter magnitudes than comparable surveys, we employ a mixture model approach to jointly characterize stream populations in proper motions, radial velocities, and metallicities against a Milky Way halo background. By applying this framework to the C-19 stellar stream, we identify a total of 47 spectroscopically confirmed member stars, of which 41 are newly identified and only 6 were previously reported in the literature. In this work, we measure a velocity dispersion of $7.8^{+1.5}_{-1.3}$ km s$^{-1}$ and a mean metallicity of [Fe/H] = $-3.36^{+0.12}_{-0.10}$. We further identify a novel 'spur' feature within the stream. We conclude that our measurements are in line with previous works identifying C-19 as a 'hot', metal-poor stream. In forthcoming work, we will apply this approach to many more streams in the DESI footprint, enabling population-level comparisons with predictions from simulations.

repl.title: Supermassive stars with embedded stellar black hole cores: dense assembling star clusters as faint multiple Little Red Dot systems
repl.summary: Numerical simulations have established that star clusters with densities comparable to the high redshift ($z>6$-$10$) James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) proto globular clusters may build up extremely massive (EMSs; $m_\mathrm{\star}>1000 M_\odot$) or even supermassive stars (SMSs; $m_\mathrm{\star}>10000 M_\odot$) and potentially intermediate mass black holes (IMBHs) through runaway stellar collisions. Using direct simulations of assembling star clusters including post-Newtonian black hole dynamics and stellar evolution, we demonstrate that in such dense environments ($\Sigma_\mathrm{h} \gtrsim 10^6 M_\odot$pc$^\mathrm{-2}$) stellar BHs ($m_\bullet \lesssim 60 M_\odot$), driven by rapid mass segregation and relaxation effects within the sphere of influence of the EMSs/SMSs, may strongly interact with the extremely massive stars and become embedded within their gaseous layers. We suggest that this quasi-star (QS) like embedded BH phase is a natural outcome of the runaway formation of EMSs/SMSs in the densest star clusters. The QS phase may be $1$-$2$ orders of magnitude longer in duration than the lifetime of the SMS, enabling an extended growth period by stellar collisions, and allows the formation of embedded gravitational wave sources if the QS captures more than a single stellar BH. The star cluster assembly region sizes ($\sim100$ pc), QS masses ($\gtrsim 10^4 M_\odot$) and their proximity to young, massive blue star forming clumps are consistent with the faint population of multiple little red dots (LRDs) recently discovered by the JWST.

repl.title: No Blue without Red: Evolutionary Properties of Super-Early Galaxies
repl.summary: The discovery of numerous luminous, super-early galaxies at $z>10$ by JWST has revealed a striking diversity in their ultraviolet (UV) properties, ranging from extremely blue, dust-poor systems to a smaller population of significantly reddened sources. We investigate the physical origin of this diversity within the framework of the Attenuation-Free Model (AFM), in which radiation-driven outflows redistribute dust to large galactic radii, reducing the effective attenuation. Starting from a sample of 32 spectroscopically confirmed super-early galaxies, we apply the detailed AFM analysis to a subset of 17 systems with suitable size constraints and derive their key physical properties, including halo mass, star formation efficiency, metallicity, and outflow extent. We find that these systems reside in massive halos ($\log M/M_\odot \sim 10.7$) and exhibit moderate ($0.01 < \epsilon_* < 0.05$) star formation efficiencies, while frequently reaching super-Eddington conditions that trigger powerful outflows. Within the AFM framework, we propose a possible evolutionary sequence in which galaxies transition from a dust-obscured ``Red Monster'' phase to a UV-bright ``Blue Monster'' phase as outflows clear their central regions. The recently confirmed red galaxy EGS-z11-R0 at $z=11.45$ is naturally interpreted as a system observed during this obscured phase. Compact ($r_e < 150$ pc) sources are instead difficult to reconcile within AFM; we speculate that their emission is dominated by an AGN. Our results provide a coherent interpretation of super-early galaxy properties and highlight the key role of radiation-driven outflows in shaping galaxy evolution at cosmic dawn. Future observations with JWST and ALMA will be essential to test these predictions and further constrain the nature of the earliest galaxies.

repl.title: Reconstructing the Globular Cluster Initial Mass Function from Present-day Globular Cluster Systems
repl.summary: The near-universal turnover mass of the present-day globular cluster mass function (GCMF), $M_{\rm TO} \sim 2 \times 10^5\ {\rm M_\odot}$, is a well established observational feature across galaxies of different types and masses, providing an important empirical benchmark for understanding the globular cluster initial mass function (GCIMF). Competing explanations of this property invoke either dynamical evolution from an initial power-law distribution or an imprint of cluster formation physics. We address this problem by reconstructing the high-mass regime of the GCIMF by inverting the mass loss due to dynamical evolution of present-day globular cluster systems across a wide range of host galaxy masses. Our method is based on an environment-dependent mass-loss model calibrated by direct $N$-body simulations in time-dependent tidal fields, enabling a mapping between observed cluster masses and their progenitor values without assuming a priori a functional form for the GCIMF. We apply our method to galaxies spanning halo masses of $\sim10^{9}$ - $10^{12}\ {\rm M_\odot}$, combining systems with individually measured globular cluster masses as well as large statistical samples constructed from observed global properties. The recovered GCIMFs are systematically shifted towards higher masses and exhibit a power-law behavior at the high-mass end. The inferred slopes vary across galaxies and show a strong correlation with host halo mass, with more massive galaxies exhibiting steeper high-mass slopes. Our results suggest that the slope of the GCIMF depends on the galactic properties and provides a direct empirical link between present-day globular cluster systems and their high-redshift progenitors.

repl.title: A Consistent Comparison of Intracluster Light Assembly in Simulations I. Redshift Evolution and Progenitor Galaxies
repl.summary: The tidal stripping of satellite galaxies and the stellar detritus ejected during galaxy mergers builds up a diffuse stellar component in galaxy clusters known as the intracluster light (ICL). We investigate ICL assembly in cluster-mass haloes ($M_{178c}\sim10^{14}-10^{15}$ M$_\odot$) using four different hydrodynamical simulations (Horizon-AGN, TNG100, The Three Hundred Gizmo-Simba 7K, and Hydrangea) under a homogenized ICL identification framework. For our fiducial ICL definition we obtain broadly consistent $z\approx0$ ICL stellar mass fractions ($\sim0.1-0.2$) and, by tracking the progenitors of $z\approx0$ clusters back to $z\gtrsim2$, find no significant evolution in average ICL mass fractions. Alternative approaches for distinguishing the ICL from the central galaxy show the absolute ICL fraction to be highly sensitive to adopted definition, but we never find any significant inter-simulation discrepancies when implementing a consistent methodology to identify the ICL. Whether the average ICL mass fraction falls with increasing redshift or does not evolve is determined by the ICL definition adopted. By tracing $z\approx0$ ICL stars back to their progenitor galaxies, we find that lower-mass satellites typically make slightly larger ICL contributions relative to their mass in every considered simulation, but which galaxies make the dominant contribution to the ICL is primarily controlled by the infalling satellite mass function. Most ICL stars sourced from satellite galaxies are therefore expected to originate from galaxies with infall stellar masses above $\sim10^{10}$ M$_\odot$ and largely within $10^{10.5}-10^{11.5}$ M$_\odot$.

repl.title: pop-cosmos: Galaxy size evolution across structural and star-formation classifications in COSMOS-Web
repl.summary: Galaxy sizes are correlated with stellar mass and redshift, as characterised by size scaling relations. The inferred forms of these scaling relations are sensitive to how galaxies are classified -- either by their star formation activity (e.g. specific star-formation rate, sSFR) or by their morphology markers (e.g. bulge-to-total ratio, Sérsic index). We combine stellar mass and sSFR estimates from pop-cosmos (a generative model trained on COSMOS2020 Spitzer IRAC $\textit{Ch.1} <26$) with size and morphology measurements from COSMOS-Web, obtaining $99,369$ galaxies. By investigating the size-mass and the size-redshift relations, we show that: (i) the sSFR/morphology splits give quantitatively different slopes, intercepts, and intrinsic scatter behaviour; (ii) intrinsic scatter depends on structural morphology but not on sSFR, which constrains the galaxy-halo connection; (iii) the quiescent and bulge-dominated size-mass relations both show double-power law breaks, but at different pivot masses, indicating that quenching and structural transformation occur on different time-scales; (iv) the morphology-dependent trends are only recoverable from space-based imaging. Further, the quiescent pivot mass $M_{\ast} \sim 10^{10.7}~\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ coincides with the mass scale at which active galactic nuclei (AGN, infrared torus) bolometric luminosity fraction peaks in transitioning galaxies, while the bulge-dominated pivot mass $M_{\ast} \sim 10^{11.1}~\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ coincides with the halo mass at which AGN-driven baryonic redistribution peaks, which may trace the interval over which AGN feedback ramps from quenching onset to structural transformation.

repl.title: Mapping Dust Attenuation at Kiloparsec Scales. III. The 2175Å Bump
repl.summary: We combine the Swift/UVOT+MaNGA catalog with 2MASS $K_s$ imaging to map the 2175Å attenuation bump at kiloparsec scales in nearby galaxies. We use two complementary estimators: an ultraviolet-to-near-infrared attenuation-curve method, yielding $A_{bump}^{UOIR}$ and $B$ for 2487 high-continuum-S/N spaxels, and the NUV-only method of \citet{2025PASA...42...22B}, yielding $A_{bump}^{NUV}$ and $k_{bump}$ for 7934 spaxels. The two absolute bump estimates agree well where they overlap. We compare bump strength with local stellar-population, emission-line, attenuation-curve, and geometric diagnostics after separating star-forming (SF) and non-SF regions. The strongest bumps occur at low specific H$\alpha$ surface brightness, $\Sigma_{\text{H}\alpha}/\Sigma_\ast$, especially in non-SF regions, where this ratio traces ionized-gas emission per unit stellar mass rather than sSFR. The bump also weakens with EW(H$\alpha$) and strengthens with $D_n4000$ and stellar age. In contrast, metallicity, inclination, galactocentric radius, $A_V$, and optical attenuation-curve slope are secondary predictors. The absolute strength $A_{bump}^{NUV}$ increases with $\Sigma_{\text{H}\alpha}$ and $\Sigma_\ast$, while the relative strengths $k_{bump}$ and $B$ do not, indicating that absolute bump amplitude partly follows dust column whereas normalized strengths better trace effective bump prominence. These results support local radiation-field processing of the 2175Å carriers.

repl.title: Evolution of Binaries Under Stochastic Perturbations
repl.summary: We develop a general Fokker-Planck framework describing the dynamical evolution of Keplerian binaries subjected to stochastic perturbations. The formalism provides an algorithmic way to obtain the Fokker-Planck drift and diffusion coefficients of any set of orbital variables given the statistics of the perturbations. We apply the method to three physically distinct regimes: adiabatic tidal perturbations, white-noise tidal perturbations, and impulsive encounters with a third body of arbitrary density profile. In each regime we provide explicit drift and diffusion coefficients for all six orbital elements, derive the associated evolution timescale, and obtain analytic steady-state distribution functions. Our results extend previous treatments by including the evolution of the binary's orientation, retaining the complete tensor structure of tidal correlators, treating non-pointlike perturbers, and resolving the exact geometry of impulsive encounters. The latter correction leads to a steady-state eccentricity distribution that is slightly sub-thermal. We also show how these equations can be applied directly in several astrophysical scenarios, including binaries perturbed by dark matter subhaloes, ultralight dark matter, and the interstellar medium. This work delivers both a complete mathematical framework and a practical toolkit for stochastic binary evolution, providing ready-to-evaluate equations to be applied directly to binary population data.

repl.title: Outflows in a super-Eddington quasar drive clumpy circumgalactic medium and extended H$α$ nebulae at $z \gtrsim 6$
repl.summary: The discovery of gargantuan black holes with masses exceeding a billion solar masses at $z\gtrsim6$ suggests rapid black hole growth and significant energy input into their host galaxies in the early Universe. With JWST probing previously unseen phases of the interstellar (ISM) and circumgalactic (CGM) medium around $z > 6$ quasars, detailed theoretical studies can now be directly confronted with observations. We use zoom-in simulations of a massive protocluster at $z\sim6$, employing both the fiducial FABLE galaxy formation model and modifications that allow earlier black hole seeding and mildly super-Eddington accretion. The central quasar remains Compton-thick throughout most of its evolution, with the obscuration arising from the ISM of its compact host galaxy. The onset of sufficiently strong quasar feedback drives a 'blow-out' episode, clearing out escape channels for ionizing radiation and leaving the central engine unobscured. This leads to a complete transformation of the CGM, whereby powerful, metal-enriched outflows produce a population of cold, fast, neutral clumps, significantly increasing the covering fraction of neutral hydrogen in the host halo. Radiative transfer calculations performed with a new ray-tracing code show that the CGM responds to quasar activity through the formation of H$\alpha$ nebulae, whose size and luminosity increase with the strength of quasar feedback and decrease with obscuration level. Enhanced early black hole growth thus fundamentally reshapes the ISM and CGM of $z\sim6$ quasars, leaving clear observable signatures in their obscuration, neutral hydrogen distribution, and extended H$\alpha$ emission.

The field-of-view in every panel covers 200 ​ kpc × 200 ​ kpc 200~{\rm kpc}~\times~200~{\rm kpc} with a projection width of 200 ​ kpc 200~{\rm kpc} , and the white circle shows the virial radius R vir ≈ 80 ​ kpc R_{\mathrm{vir}}\approx 80~{\rm kpc} . repl.title: Variations in the 3.3 $μ$m Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon Feature Across Nearby Galaxies Driven by Metallicity and Radiation Field Spectrum
repl.summary: We use JWST NIRCam imaging to investigate the 3.3 ${\mu}$m polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) feature in nearby galaxies. NIRCam observations of the 3.3 ${\mu}$m feature are emerging as a powerful tool for studying the structure of the interstellar medium (ISM) and the conditions of the dust at ~0".1 resolution. These maps require accurate subtraction of the underlying continuum emission. We present an empirical method to isolate the PAH-correlated emission in the F335M filter using the F300M and F360M filters for continuum subtraction. We find that the slope of the F335M/F300M versus F360M/F300M colors for PAH-correlated emission shows a dependence on local ISM properties, with the strongest dependence on specific star formation rate. Weaker emission features captured by these bands appear suppressed relative to the main 3.3 ${\mu}$m feature in regions of active star formation. We find trends in the 3.3/7.7 and 3.3/11.3 ${\mu}$m ratios that suggest changes in PAH size, charge, and heating by a varying radiation field spectrum. We find decreases in both band ratios with increasing metallicity, which we attribute to a shift to smaller PAH populations at low metallicity. Comparison to optical ionized gas line ratios and dust models show that variations in the interstellar radiation field spectrum influence the PAH feature ratios. This analysis supports inhibited growth formation scenarios for the observed PAH band ratio trends with metallicity and emphasizes the importance of considering the local radiation field characteristics and gas-phase metallicity when using these band ratios as PAH property diagnostics.

repl.title: Energy Partitioning in Dust-catalyzed $\mathrm{H_2}$ and HD Formation Revealed by Molecular Simulations Considering Nuclear Quantum Effects
repl.summary: Molecular hydrogen formation on interstellar dust grains is a key surface process, but the partitioning of recombination energy between the substrate and the nascent molecule remains poorly understood. Here, we use ring-polymer molecular dynamics (RPMD) with a machine-learning force field to investigate energy partitioning during H2 and HD formation on graphene at T=25 K, 50 K and 100 K, focusing on the chemisorbed-H recombination pathway previously identified as the dominant low-temperature channel on bare graphitic surfaces when nuclear quantum effects are included. The desorbing molecule retains approximately 84-87% of the effective released energy, with only weak variation across the three velocity-initialization temperatures under the present sampling protocol. Within the retained molecular energy, rovibrational motion dominates at 25 K, whereas center-of-mass translation becomes increasingly important at 100 K. H2 and HD show similar total energy retention, with modest isotope-dependent differences in their internal partitioning. The effective joint rovibrational distributions show a modest positive association between vibrational and rotational excitation. Purely radiative cascade calculations in the optically thin, collision-free limit yield formation-pumping spectra at all three temperatures. From 25 to 100 K, the rovibrational fraction of the emitted energy decreases from approximately 43% to 28% for H2 and from 41% to 28% for HD, while the strongest lines remain in similar wavelength regions. These results provide an energy-resolved microscopic picture of surface-mediated energy redistribution and formation pumping in H2/HD formation on graphene.

repl.title: Improved constraints on the Milky Way potential using the M68 stream and DESI spectroscopic data
repl.summary: We present a selection of stars belonging to the stellar stream of the M68 (NGC 4590) globular cluster, also known as Fjörm. This star selection is an improvement on previous ones that used only Gaia data, as it incorporates spectroscopic measurements from the DESI survey and photometric data from the DESI Legacy Surveys. The selection contains 96 stars, each with five phase-space parameters from Gaia-DR3 and radial velocity from DESI, covering the entire observed section of the stream. This constitutes the largest selection of M68 stream stars with measured radial velocities to date. The observed stream is wider than expected from N-body simulations, and the stars farthest from the centre of the stream appear to be correlated in radial velocity space. This suggests that these stars cannot have been stripped from the cluster in a static axisymmetric potential. By modelling a mock sample of stream stars created using an N-body simulation, we found that we could reliably constrain the disc mass $M_{\rm d}$ and the dark matter halo axis ratio $q_{\rm h}$ of the Milky Way. This is because the stream flows close to and almost parallel to the disc. Using the 44 stars that are consistent with having been stripped from the cluster, combined with measurements of the Milky Way's rotation curve, we constrain the Galactic potential, obtaining $M_{\rm d} = 5.34 \pm 0.57 \times 10^{10}$ M$_{\rm sun}$ and an oblate halo of $q_{\rm h} = 0.83^{+0.06}_{-0.05}$. Additionally, by fitting the stream track, we estimate the Heliocentric distance of M68 to be $r=10.55\pm0.09$ kpc.

repl.title: A posteriori correction of Gaia CRF proper motions using conditional probability and zero-parallax prior
repl.summary: The formal precision of Gaia CRF proper motions, and in principle positions, can be statistically improved by introducing conditional probability based on the zero-parallax prior for these extremely distant sources. The method developed in this study produces statistically conditioned proper-motion estimates under the assumed per-source Gaussian covariance model. It is demonstrated that thus corrected proper motion vectors of 1.2 million CRF objects in Gaia DR3 show a tighter distribution around zero and a general reduction in the rate of outliers by approximately 15\%. A general vector spherical harmonic fit to degree 4 is produced with the corrected data for a filtered subset of CRF quasars with redshifts between 1 and 1.5. This application, predicated on the unknown stochastic component of the global parallax field, shows a 3-sigma change in the estimated magnitude of the Galactocentric acceleration of the solar system barycenter, quantifying the sensitivity of this fundamental determination to the proposed conditioning of proper motions.

repl.title: Super-Eddington Accretion and Early-Stage Feedback in Ton S180
repl.summary: Narrow-line Seyfert 1 (NLSy1) galaxies are key laboratories for studying rapid supermassive black hole (SMBH) growth and active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback at high accretion rates. We investigate the nearby NLSy1 Ton S180 with VLT-MUSE optical integral field spectroscopy to connect its nuclear accretion properties with the spatially resolved ionized gas and host-galaxy kinematics. We modeled the unresolved nuclear spectrum and applied a custom point spread function subtraction to recover the host-galaxy emission on kiloparsec scales. The nuclear spectrum requires a complex permitted-line decomposition and a blueshifted [O III] outflow component. Single-epoch estimators and the stellar velocity dispersion imply black hole masses in the range $\log(M_{\rm BH}/M_\odot) = 6.5 - 7.7$. Combined with the observed luminosity, this implies a dimensionless mass accretion rate of $\dot{M} / \dot{M}_{\rm Edd} = 4.1 - 980$, confirming the extreme accretion regime. The host galaxy shows a circumnuclear ring, an inner elongated structure consistent with a bar, and rotation-dominated gas and stellar kinematics. Simple inflow models do not significantly better reproduce the observed velocity field. We detect a resolved ionized outflow extending about 2 kpc west of the nucleus, with mildly blueshifted velocities (with a maximum of $v_{\rm max} \sim 340$ km s$^{-1}$). Its mass outflow rate is only $\sim 4.2 \times 10^{-4}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, whereas the unresolved nuclear outflow reaches $v_{\rm max} \sim 1140$ km s$^{-1}$ and $\dot{M}_{\rm out} > 1.5\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. This contrast may reflect either weak ionized coupling from nuclear to galactic scales or different episodes of AGN activity over time. These results show that Ton S180 is undergoing rapid SMBH growth, while the observed ionized outflow remains confined to the inner few kiloparsecs and is weak on host-galaxy scales.
